title: Balanced dense NFA Acceptance Hypothesis
formal: For the balanced dense binary NFA acceptance problem and word-RAM model below, is it true that for every constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) no uniform randomized algorithm has worst-case running time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) and error at most \(1/3\) on every input?
definitions:
An instance supplies \(n\ge2\), states \(Q=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), a start state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), transitions \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\), and an explicit binary word \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\) of length exactly \(n\). There are no empty-word transitions and no repeated copies of a transition. Require \(n^2\le|\Delta|\le2n^2\). The transition relation is given as two \(n\times n\) Boolean matrices, with entry \((a,b)\) for symbol \(s\) indicating whether \((a,s,b)\in\Delta\). The accepting set is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. The word is accepted exactly when \[ \exists q_1,\ldots,q_n\in Q:\quad q_n\in F\ \text{ and }\ \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ (q_{j-1},x_j,q_j)\in\Delta.\]

The matrices are stored in row-major order, one Boolean entry per word; \(n,q_0\), the indicator entries and the input characters likewise occupy one word each in a fixed layout. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), where the fixed integer \(d\ge8\) is chosen with the algorithm. The input is read-only, random-access memory; auxiliary memory initially contains zeros. Its addresses and individual values fit in one word. The algorithm is a fixed finite program with no advice or precomputed input-dependent data.

Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions. Each random instruction returns an independent uniform \(w\)-bit word. All initialization, preprocessing, table construction and final output are charged. Arbitrary algebraic algorithms in this instruction model are allowed; no combinatorial restriction is imposed.

Correctness means that for every valid fixed input, the output equals its acceptance bit with probability at least \(2/3\). Running time is a worst-case bound over valid inputs and all random choices, not an expected bound. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), a putative algorithm, \(d\), and constants \(C,n_0\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input. The excluded guarantee is that all valid instances with \(n\ge n_0\) terminate within \(C n^{3-\varepsilon}\) instructions while every valid instance, including smaller ones, is correctly decided with the stated error.

context_blocks.text: The automaton records possible state changes under each symbol. Acceptance asks whether one possible trajectory follows the entire supplied word and ends in an accepting state. Here both the number of states and the word length grow together, and the transition relation has quadratic size.

The 2024 source formulates a broader hypothesis with transition count \(\Theta(n^\alpha)\), word length \(\Theta(n^\beta)\), and a subpolynomial alphabet. It identifies \(\alpha=2,\beta=1\) as a core regime. This card retains its previously selected specialization to a binary alphabet, exactly \(n\) symbols, and the explicit density interval \([n^2,2n^2]\). It does not identify that one proposition with every parameter regime of the broader hypothesis.

The elementary bound in this balanced regime is \(O(n^3)\). The source reports subpolynomial-factor improvements for dense automata, which are compatible with excluding every fixed power saving. Its sparse-automaton bounds use SETH, and its combinatorial lower bounds have a restricted algorithm model. Neither type constitutes the unconditional all-algorithm lower bound requested here.

The broader framework connects automaton acceptance to context-free language reachability, Word Break and the online matrix-vector multiplication hypothesis. These are consequences of the source’s stated hypothesis and reductions; they should not be attributed without qualification to every editorially restricted variant.

Bille and Gørtz study the amount of nondeterministic activity during a particular regular-expression simulation. That density differs from the number of transitions in a general dense NFA. Their work explains the researcher connection recorded at import, rather than authorship of the NFA Acceptance hypothesis.

why: This is a central unresolved barrier for general automata simulation with consequences across language processing and fine-grained complexity.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A refutation supplies some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform algorithm in the stated RAM model, and proofs of its worst-case time and per-input correctness guarantees on all promised instances. A positive answer excludes all such algorithms without an unproved complexity assumption. The negation of this asymptotic statement is not a single hard or easy finite instance. A bound restricted to combinatorial or deterministic algorithms, or a subpolynomial improvement of cubic time, does not meet the target.

references.locator: Revision 7, 6 November 2023; abstract and revision history checked. Density counts activity during simulation and is not the transition density used by this card.

progress.text: The published framework states the NFA Acceptance hypothesis, its dense form, and the balanced core regime; lower bounds and implications are conditional as specified there.
The checked revision of Sparse Regular Expression Matching gives a simulation-density parameter and conditional lower bounds in a different input model.

status_note: The NFA Acceptance hypothesis is stated in the 2024 final paper. ICALP 2026 Article 135, Section 2.2 still presents it as a hypothesis; this is evidence of continued use, not a proof of the precise binary, exact-length, density-restricted proposition here. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching resolution. Source theorem scopes and the retained editorial specialization were checked; no cited proof has been independently verified in Lean.

sentences: A binary word of length equal to the number of automaton states must be tested for acceptance.
The automaton has quadratically many transitions and is supplied explicitly without preprocessing.
The question excludes every fixed polynomial improvement over cubic running time for randomized word-RAM algorithms.
The source relates a broader NFA Acceptance hypothesis to major static and dynamic complexity barriers.
This card keeps the balanced dense binary specialization separate from sparse-automaton results and from simulation-density bounds for regular expressions.
